meta.regime: Three things define the board into this week. First, the US long end is still the organising fact: the ten-year closed Friday at 5.2830%, up 4.1 basis points on a day September payrolls printed 29K against an 89K forecast, and DXY finished at 101.932 and up 0.95% on the week. The repricing that followed was a shift in timing, not direction - CME FedWatch now has an October 28 hike near 17% while December 9 carries roughly 65%, so the hike was moved rather than removed. Second, and new, the energy premium drew a coordinated policy response: on October 2 the G7 and partners agreed with the IEA to release up to 100 million barrels of crude and diesel over four months, front-loaded with a heavy diesel component in the first 20 days. The market's answer is the tradeable part. WTI fell about 4% intraday to roughly 89.15 and Brent 2.6% to about 99.63, then Brent closed at 102.250 and down just 0.06% while WTI settled 91.110 and down 1.90%. A Brent market that round-trips the largest coordinated release since March is telling you the premium is structural, and Goldman Sachs reckons the release offsets only about half the recent diesel move. Third, the week's genuine repricing was British rather than American. Market odds of a November 5 Bank Rate hike now run from about 75% to 88% against 70% before Governor Bailey spoke, Deputy Governors Breeden and Lombardelli have both signalled they are moving toward a hike, and the gilt ten-year is at 5.3770% and a near two-decade high. That is what lifts GBP to +2 and makes the euro-sterling cross the cleanest expression on the page.

The denser cluster for this board is October 8, when the ECB publishes the September accounts at 11:30Z and Greene, Pill and Lombardelli all speak - Lombardelli being one of the two swing votes on the BoE. Canada employment on October 9 at 12:30Z is the week's only red folder carrying figures.

dailyRead: Markets are shut, Friday's closes are the last prints on the board, and the honest thing to say is that the most useful work this weekend was not re-reading the US tape but noticing that the week's real repricing happened in sterling and almost nobody led with it. Start with what has not changed, because it matters. The ten-year closed at 5.2830%, up 4.1 basis points on a day that September payrolls missed on all three legs - 29K against an 89K forecast, unemployment at 4.2%, average hourly earnings 0.1% m/m - and DXY closed at 101.932, up 0.95% on the week and 3.06% on the month. A bond market that sells off on weak employment data is pricing issuance and persistent inflation rather than the next meeting, and the pricing now puts a number on it that yesterday's report did not: CME FedWatch has an October 28 hike near 17%, with Kalshi and Polymarket in the same place at roughly 17% hike against 84% hold, while December 9 carries about 65% and CME has a 65.9% chance the target range sits at 4.00-4.25% after that meeting. That is a cleaner statement of the same call - the dollar stays at +2, October is gone, December is the live meeting and it is better than a coin flip. The September SEP is still the structural support: four 2026 dots at a 4.375% midpoint, twelve at 4.125%, two at 3.875%, the median revised up to 4.1% from 3.8% in June, and 17 of 18 participants placing PCE inflation risks to the upside. Now the part that changes. Sterling has been sitting at +1 on this board with an explicit justification: the Bank of England's own July Market Participants Survey still had a median of 3.75% after November 5, so I was not willing to pay up for the hawkish case. That reasoning is now stale and the instruction to prefer rate-market pricing over my own prior framing applies squarely to it. Market odds on a November 5 hike run from about 75% to 88% depending on the source, with one read at 80.5% against 70% before Bailey spoke, and LSEG has investors pricing four hikes by July 2027. More importantly the vote arithmetic has moved. September was 6-3 with Pill, Mann and Greene wanting 4.00%, and the two names that matter among the six holders have now shifted: Breeden says a hike would be appropriate if second-round effects crystallise, Lombardelli says the case for raising Bank Rate is building. Five of the six holders have now set out conditions for a hike and only two need to switch. Against that the gilt ten-year is 5.3770%, above the US ten-year and a near two-decade high, the energy pass-through is mechanical rather than market-dependent with UK gas at 188.10 GBp/thm and up 154.84% year to date and the domestic unit rate stepping from 6.29p to 8p per kWh on October 1, and the tape agrees: GBP/USD was -0.05% on the week against a dollar that took about 1% out of everything else. So GBP goes to +2 and STRENGTHENING, EUR/GBP becomes a HIGH-conviction short at 0.85001 after falling 1.15% on the week, GBP/NZD becomes the cleanest non-dollar long on the board at a three-point score gap, and GBP/USD becomes a RANGE because both legs are now +2 - which is what the flat week was already telling me. The three BoE speakers on October 8, Lombardelli among them, are the specific thing to watch. The oil story is the other genuinely new development and it cuts two ways, so name both. On October 2 the G7 and partner countries agreed with the IEA to release up to 100 million barrels of crude and diesel over four months, beginning immediately and front-loaded with a substantial diesel release across the first 20 days, alongside coordinated refinery maintenance and a commitment not to restrict energy trade; Reuters reported the US had demanded France and Germany draw on emergency diesel reserves and threatened to ban diesel exports if they refused. That is a real supply response and WTI took it, falling about 4% intraday to roughly 89.15 before settling 91.110 and down 1.90%. What Brent did is the more useful observation: it fell 2.6% to about 99.63 and then closed at 102.250, down 0.06%, up 4.94% on the week and 7.05% on the month. A waterborne market that fully round-trips a 100 million barrel coordinated release is not a market whose premium is about to break, and Goldman Sachs estimates the release offsets only around half the recent diesel rise. The reason it holds is on the other side of the ledger: Iranian loadings were zero in September with about 15 million barrels left on the water, nearly all bound for China, leaving Tehran roughly two weeks from having nothing to trade; five ships were struck in a 72-hour stretch late last week including a supertanker that caught fire off Oman; and Trump rejected Iran's seven-day ceasefire and phased-reopening proposal while naming the November 3 midterms as the point after which strikes are possible. So USOIL stays a RANGE and the Brent-WTI spread at $11.14 stays the honest description of where the risk is priced, but the skew inside that range is now upward rather than neutral, and I would not be short crude into a release the market has already rejected. The knock-on is that Canada gets less help than a 102-dollar Brent print suggests, because the release lands on exactly the barrels Canada sells. USD/CAD is the cleanest dollar long on the board at 1.42539, up 0.79% on the week and 3.33% on the month, against the widest clean policy gap here - 2.25% after seven consecutive holds against a 4.00% Fed upper bound - and August employment at -41.7K. Thursday is the test: October 9 at 12:30Z is the week's only red folder with figures, and the consensus is +9.0K employment with the unemployment rate rising to 6.5% from 6.4%. A second negative print makes this a conviction short of the loonie; a bounce to +9K or better with oil firm is the specific thing that takes the conviction down. Europe stays pinned and the reason is still fiscal rather than monetary. September flash HICP at 3.8% y/y is the highest since September 2023 with energy inflation at 18.8% from 14.3%, roughly 1.7 points of the headline, and the ECB still has at least two more hikes priced - yet the euro was the worst major of the week at -1.20%. Lecornu's 2027 draft budget, presented October 1, freezes public-sector wages and all but the lowest pensions, splits the consolidation roughly 60/40 between spending cuts and revenue, and takes the deficit only from 5.4% to 5.0% of GDP with a return to the EU's 3% threshold deferred to 2029; it faces a divided parliament that has already removed one Macron prime minister, and the budget landed alongside violent student protests. The market's verdict is in the spread: the OAT closed at 4.8656% against a Bund at 3.4545%, about 141 basis points and the widest since the 2012 euro-area crisis, and France now trades wide of both Italy at 4.6107% and Greece at 4.5247%. EUR stays at 0 and MIXED - the policy leg is genuinely hawkish and the fiscal leg genuinely bad, and moving the score again one day after cutting it to 0 on this same evidence would be noise rather than analysis. The ECB accounts on October 8 at 11:30Z are the scheduled read. The yen keeps +1 and MIXED, and the dispersion is the answer rather than a number. October 30 pricing runs from 20-30% on former executive director Momma's read, through 25.6% as of September 30, to about 56% in one market assessment, and the thing that reconciles them is that money markets price roughly 90 basis points of cumulative BoJ hikes over twelve months - the path is hawkish even where the October meeting is not. MUFG notes several board members favour accelerating hikes or moving faster toward neutral, and the September decision was itself a 7-2 vote with Asada and Sato dissenting against the hike, which is a split board rather than a reluctant one. Against that, 1.25% versus a 5.2830% US ten-year is still the worst funding disadvantage here, and USD/JPY at 157.856 and up 0.38% on the week reflects it. Ueda speaks October 6 at 06:35Z and is the one scheduled event that can move October back onto the table. The antipodeans are both holds with an honest caveat each. For New Zealand the October 28 estimates are not merely dispersed, they are contradictory: one tracker has an 88% hold, another has roughly 80% for a hike to 3.00%, and the RBNZ's own September track implies about 30%. I am not going to pick one, so NZD keeps the -1 the tape has earned - worst major on the month at -4.52%, unemployment 5.6% - with the forward lean at range. The resolvable fact is that the Bank's own forecast has Q3 inflation easing to 3.9% from 4.1%, so the October 21 CPI is a clean test against a published number, and Governor Breman has already said elevated oil could push near-term inflation past the September forecast. For Australia the copper leg is more interesting than its price. Copper closed at 6.4920 a pound, up 0.15% on the day but down 3.10% on the week and about 4% below its September record, which looks bearish until you read the supply side: BHP's Escondida, the world's largest copper mine, halted all operations on September 23 after a contractor was killed, removing roughly 3,455 tonnes a day, and its supervisors have since voted 95% to authorise a strike, with mandatory mediation to run first. Shanghai inventories are low into the October 1-8 Golden Week holiday and the LME prompt spread sat at a monthly high on Chinese Q4 smelter maintenance. A market that cannot rally on that is a market where the dollar and energy costs are beating physical tightness, which is exactly why copper is a RANGE and not a long, and why AUD stays at 0 despite the highest policy rate on the board at 4.60% and a unanimous 9-0 September hike. The franc keeps the -1 it was raised to yesterday and the week supports it rather than contradicting it: USD/CHF rose just 0.06% while EUR/CHF fell 1.14%, AUD/CHF 0.88%, NZD/CHF 0.79% and CAD/CHF 0.72%. Gold fell 3.38% on the week and silver 6.06% while the strait stayed shut, so the haven bid has migrated out of bullion and into the currency, and TE's own SNB summary confirms the Bank still says it remains willing to intervene in FX as necessary. With no SNB meeting until December 10 the franc has no domestic catalyst for ten weeks and trades Hormuz; the October 22 minutes are the only scheduled Swiss item. Bullion stays short on the same logic that lifted the franc: a 5.2830% nominal ten-year with the TIPS real yield edging toward 2.5% taxes a non-yielding haven, and gold is -7.45% on the month and -4.16% year to date with silver -9.85% and -15.29%. The two European indices need separating, and this is where the oil release does real work. Friday flattered both - the DAX closed 25,231 and up 1.17%, the Euro Stoxx 50 at 6,242 and up 1.07% after hitting a three-and-a-half-month low - and TE attributes both moves to cheaper oil, the reserve release and falling bond yields, with the Bund down 6.6 basis points to 3.4545%. For the DAX that is a genuine change to the thesis: the short was an energy-cost short, and a coordinated 100 million barrel release is the specific thing that undermines it, so GER40 comes off SHORT to RANGE at low-to-medium conviction with the index still -2.97% on the month and German gas at 75.77 and up 130.95% year on year as the cap. The EU50 does not get the same treatment, because its dominating leg is its own: banking was among the sectors that lagged on a 1.07% up day, per TE's own summary, and banks are its heaviest weight. An index whose largest sector will not participate in its own relief rally, while carrying French sovereign risk the DAX does not, is the weaker of the two, so EU50 stays SHORT at medium. The cleanest tickets into the week: EUR/GBP short and GBP/NZD long on the sterling repricing, USD/CAD long into Thursday's Canadian jobs, and EUR/USD short - with the standing caveat that EUR/USD, USD/CAD and DXY are one dollar trade in three costumes and should be sized as one, while the sterling pair is the genuinely independent position.

GBP.note: TE re-verified: Bank Rate is 3.75%, held at the September 17 decision on a 6-3 vote with three members preferring 4.00%, the same split as July. TE's summary records the MPC saying prolonged Middle East conflict has pushed energy prices higher and contributed to UK CPI rising to 3.1% in August, with further increases expected in coming quarters, and that policy must ensure inflation returns sustainably to 2% while the Committee assesses the scale and duration of the energy shock; it notes limited evidence so far of significant second-round effects on wages and prices, with that risk increasing if energy costs stay elevated. The MPC also unanimously agreed to run the gilt stock to zero over a multi-year programme at an average GBP46 billion a year through 2034. What has changed since yesterday is the vote arithmetic and the pricing, and it is why this report stops relying on the Bank's July Market Participants Survey median of 3.75%. Deputy Governor Breeden has said a hike would be appropriate if second-round effects crystallise, and Deputy Governor Lombardelli that the case for raising Bank Rate is building; both voted to hold in September, so with five of the six holders having now set out conditions for a hike, only two need to switch for a majority. LSEG data has investors pricing four hikes by July 2027. The gilt ten-year is 5.3770%, above the US ten-year at 5.2830% and a near two-decade high. The energy pass-through is mechanical rather than market-dependent: UK gas is 188.10 GBp/thm, up 2.76% on the week and 154.84% year to date, and the domestic unit rate stepped from 6.29p to 8p per kWh on October 1, about 27% higher year on year. The soft leg is labour, with the claimant count having risen and TE's payroll proxy at -26.1K. Four MPC speakers this week: Mann October 6 at 08:30Z, then Greene at 09:15Z, Pill at 10:30Z and Lombardelli at 13:00Z on October 8 - Lombardelli being one of the two swing votes. October 20 average earnings and October 21 CPI then settle it before November 5 at 12:00Z.

JPY.when: October 29-30 is live but not favoured and December is the better base case; the dispersion is wide, from 20-30% through 25.6% to about 56% depending on the source, while twelve-month pricing carries roughly 90 basis points of hikes
JPY.note: TE re-verified: the policy rate is 1.25% after the September 18 hike, the highest since April 1995. The vote detail is new on this board and matters: TE records it as a 7-2 decision with Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato dissenting against the hike, taken just three months after the previous increase - the shortest interval between BoJ hikes since 1990 - and following pressure from Washington including calls from US Treasury Secretary Bessent for higher rates. TE notes most policymakers signalled support for further increases and that the Bank expects inflation above 2% in coming years, with analysts looking for price growth near 3% by early next year. The October dispersion is the honest answer rather than a single number: former executive director Kazuo Momma puts an October hike at 20-30%, one tracker had 25.6% as of September 30, and another market assessment reads about 56%. What reconciles them is the twelve-month path - money markets price roughly 90 basis points of cumulative hikes - so the direction is not in question and the timing is. MUFG notes several board members favour accelerating hikes or moving more quickly toward neutral, while cautioning that Ueda's messaging may struggle to match the pace swaps discount. The October 30 meeting carries a fresh quarterly Outlook Report, which remains the natural vehicle for a hike the Bank wants its own forecasts to justify. The drag is unchanged and structural: 1.25% against a 5.2830% US ten-year is the worst funding disadvantage on this board, and the JGB ten-year at 3.1113% has not closed it. Tokyo core CPI printed 2.7% y/y against a 2.4% forecast with the core-core gauge at 3.0%, and the yen bid from it faded inside the hour. Ueda speaks October 6 at 06:35Z - a red folder and the one scheduled chance to put October back - with average cash earnings the same day at 23:30Z.

AUD.when: November 3, where markets have had roughly one in three since the September 29 hike; Q3 CPI on October 28 at 00:30Z resolves it
AUD.note: TE re-verified: the cash rate is 4.60% after a unanimous September 29 hike, the fourth of 2026 and the highest since 2011. TE's summary records the Board noting that higher global energy prices following oil supply disruptions amid the Middle East conflict, stronger-than-expected recent inflation and persistent domestic capacity constraints are adding to inflation, with AI-related demand lifting global technology goods prices and firms reporting rising costs and plans to pass them on; output growth slowed but was slightly stronger than expected in Q2 while consumer spending is easing, housing prices fell in most capital cities and labour market conditions have now also eased. The Board said further tightening may be needed to prevent inflation becoming embedded. The data behind it: monthly CPI 4.0% y/y for August against a 4.1% forecast and 3.5% prior with the trimmed mean at 3.6%, both above the 2-3% band; unemployment 4.6% from 4.5%; August employment +39,493; wage growth 3.2%; annual GDP 2.1% from 2.5%. The commodity leg is the one that will not confirm. Copper closed 6.4920 a pound, up 0.15% on the day but down 3.10% on the week and about 4% below its September record, despite BHP's Escondida having halted all operations on September 23 after a contractor was killed - roughly 3,455 tonnes a day removed - and its supervisors voting 95% to authorise a strike, with mandatory mediation to run first. Shanghai stocks are low into the October 1-8 Golden Week and the LME prompt spread sat at a monthly high on Chinese Q4 smelter maintenance. Employment on October 15 at 00:30Z is the near risk; the Australian ten-year is 5.3280%.

NZD.when: October 28, but with genuinely contradictory estimates rather than a consensus: one tracker reads an 88% hold, another about 80% for a hike to 3.00%, and the RBNZ's own September track implies roughly 30%
NZD.note: TE re-verified: the official cash rate is 2.75% after the September 2 hike, a second straight increase. TE's summary records the Committee framing it as gradually removing stimulus to bring inflation back to the 2% midpoint while supporting growth and employment, noting annual inflation rose to 4.1% in Q2 2026 largely on higher fuel prices from the Middle East conflict, while core inflation, wage growth and inflation expectations remain consistent with a return to the 1-3% band by mid-2027; the economy has likely resumed its recovery after lacklustre Q2 growth, though weak income growth, job insecurity and flat house prices weigh on household spending. The honest statement about October 28 is that the published estimates conflict, and the dispersion is itself the information - so this stays on hold as the Bank's own guidance implies while the score keeps the negative the tape has earned. The resolvable fact is better than any of the probabilities: the RBNZ's own forecast has Q3 inflation easing to 3.9% from 4.1%, which makes Q3 CPI on October 21 at 21:45Z a clean test against a published number, and Governor Breman has already said elevated oil could push near-term inflation past the September forecast. A print at or above 4.1% turns the hawkish market read into the base case; a print near or below 3.9% vindicates the track. Supporting data: unemployment 5.6% from 5.4%, Q2 employment +0.5%, annual GDP 2.6% from 1.7%, core inflation 3.2%, wage growth 2.1%. The carry disadvantage survives either outcome - even a hike to 3.00% leaves the OCR a full point below the Fed's upper bound - and the ten-year is 5.0687%.

CAD.when: October 28, no longer a formality: pricing has run from about 94% for a hold before the September 2 decision to somewhere between a coin flip and 74% depending on the instrument. October 9 employment and October 19 CPI settle it
CAD.note: TE re-verified: the overnight rate is 2.25% after a seventh consecutive hold on September 2, a 175 basis point gap to the Fed's upper bound and the widest clean policy gap on this board. TE's summary records the Governing Council noting a broad Q2 recovery and some resilience since the Middle East war lifted energy prices and long-maturity domestic yields, while flagging stronger upside inflation risks from the continuation of the war and the reintroduction of aggressive US tariffs on Canadian exports; underlying inflation has so far held at target despite the energy shock, and the Bank reiterated that the uncertain outlook prevents clear policy signals this year. The domestic data are weak: August employment -41.7K with full-time -35.9K after +75.1K, unemployment 6.4%, CPI 3.0% y/y with core 2.4% and the monthly rate at -0.1%, annual GDP 1.1% from 0.1%. This week is the test and it is the only red folder on the board carrying figures: September employment on October 9 at 12:30Z, where consensus is +9.0K after -41.7K with the unemployment rate seen rising to 6.5% from 6.4%. The terms-of-trade story got worse rather than better. Brent is 102.250 and up 4.94% on the week but WTI is 91.110 and down 1.90% on the day, an $11.14 spread, and the G7's 100 million barrel release lands on exactly the barrels Canada sells - the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve and refined products rather than waterborne crude. CPI with the Business Outlook Survey follows October 19, then the decision, Monetary Policy Report and Macklem press conference on October 28 at 14:30Z. The Canadian ten-year is 3.9450%.

CHF.when: December 10, ten weeks away, which leaves the franc with no domestic catalyst at all; the September minutes on October 22 at 07:30Z are the only scheduled Swiss item
CHF.note: TE re-verified: the SNB policy rate is 0.00%, held on September 24 and at zero since mid-2025. TE's summary records policymakers calling the current stance appropriate for price stability, noting inflation has risen further since June - to 0.8% in August from 0.6% in May, driven mainly by higher energy prices - and expecting it to rise further in Q4 before easing through 2027, with average inflation forecast at 0.7% for 2026 and 0.8% for both 2027 and 2028. GDP growth is seen at 1.5-2% in 2026 and around 1.5% in 2027, with high uncertainty flagged from Middle East tensions, global growth, trade policy and exchange rates. Crucially, TE records that the SNB said it remains willing to intervene in foreign exchange markets as necessary - the standard wording, restored after the franc weakened about 3% trade-weighted since June. The current data: September CPI 1.0% y/y from 0.8% with core 0.5%, annual GDP 2.3% from 0.4%, unemployment 3.0%, employment +0.5% y/y, wage growth 0.4%. What the franc actually trades is the haven bid, and last week it won that competition: USD/CHF rose only 0.06% while EUR/CHF fell 1.14%, AUD/CHF 0.88%, NZD/CHF 0.79% and CAD/CHF 0.72%, at the same time as gold fell 3.38% and silver 6.06%. With a 5.2830% US ten-year taxing non-yielding bullion, the haven flow has moved into the currency, and a zero policy rate against that yield is what caps the franc rather than what sinks it. The Swiss ten-year is 0.5250%. Gov Board Member Martin speaks October 8 at 08:05Z; Swiss unemployment is October 6 at 07:00Z and foreign currency reserves October 7.

strength.tag: Held at 0 deliberately, one day after being cut from +1: France now trades wide of Italy and Greece, but the hawkish inflation leg is equally real and moving the score twice on one set of facts would be noise
strength.drivers: Deposit facility rate 2.50% after the September 10 hike, with TE recording Lagarde placing inflation risks to the upside and growth risks to the downside; September flash HICP 3.8% y/y, the highest since September 2023, up from 3.2% and above a 3.6-3.7% consensus, with core 2.5% and energy inflation 18.8% from 14.3% contributing roughly 1.7 points; the market still prices at least two more hikes this cycle; unemployment 6.4%; annual GDP 1.2%; wage growth 3.0%; EUR/USD 1.12556, -1.20% on the week and -3.19% on the month, the worst major of the week; French ten-year 4.8656% against a Bund at 3.4545%, about 141bp and the widest since 2012, wide of Italy at 4.6107% and Greece at 4.5247%; Lecornu's 2027 budget freezes public-sector wages and all but the lowest pensions, splits consolidation roughly 60/40, trims the deficit only from 5.4% to 5.0% of GDP, defers the EU 3% threshold to 2029 and carries debt at 121.7%.
strength.forward: ⚖️ Range into October 29, genuinely two-sided. The hawkish leg is a three-year-high inflation print that makes the argument that higher bond yields are doing the ECB's tightening hard to sustain, plus a market that still expects at least two more hikes. The leg beating it is fiscal and outside the Council's control: a budget that only reaches a 5.0% deficit after austerity, an extra EUR10bn of debt service attributed to the geopolitical backdrop, a divided parliament that has already unseated one Macron prime minister, and violent student protests. When a currency cannot rally on a three-year-high inflation print, the binding constraint is somewhere else. The accounts of the September 10 meeting on October 8 at 11:30Z are the single most useful scheduled read, with Nagel on October 5. Turns bullish on hawkish accounts plus credible budget progress; turns bearish on the OAT spread widening through 150bp.

The mediation outcome at Escondida is the specific asymmetry worth watching: a short disruption resolved in mediation leaves supply intact, a month-long stoppage against roughly 39 days of global inventory cover is a different shock entirely. Q3 CPI on October 28 at 00:30Z is the resolution; employment on October 15 at 00:30Z is the near risk.

Twelve-month pricing of about 90 basis points says the direction is settled and only the timing is open.

catalysts.note: Two things land together. The RBA is priced at roughly one in three after the unanimous 9-0 September hike to 4.60%, with Q3 CPI on October 28 deciding it. Separately this is the date Trump named as the point after which renewed strikes on Iran are possible, which makes it the dated escalation risk for oil, gold and the franc - and the reason USOIL is a range with an upward skew rather than a neutral one.

catalysts.event: Bank of England interest rate decision and vote split (Bank of England)
catalysts.note: The meeting behind today's sterling upgrade, priced at roughly 75-88% for a hike against 70% before Bailey spoke. The arithmetic is the point: September was 6-3, five of the six holders have set out conditions for a hike, and Breeden and Lombardelli have both now signalled they are moving - so only two need to switch. LSEG has four hikes priced by July 2027. October 20 earnings and October 21 CPI are the two prints that decide it.

catalysts.event: Fed interest rate decision (FOMC)
catalysts.note: The live meeting now that October is priced near 17%. CME gives roughly 65% odds of a hike and a 65.9% probability the target range sits at 4.00-4.25% afterwards. The SEP backing is unchanged: sixteen of eighteen dots want at least one more 2026 hike, four want two, and the median 2026 projection was revised up to 4.1% from 3.8% in June.

catalysts.event: G7 and IEA release of up to 100 million barrels of crude and diesel over four months
catalysts.note: Agreed October 2 and beginning immediately, front-loaded with a substantial diesel component across the first 20 days, alongside coordinated refinery maintenance and a commitment not to restrict energy trade; Reuters reported the US had demanded France and Germany draw on emergency diesel reserves and threatened to ban diesel exports if they refused. The market's response is the tradeable part: WTI fell about 4% intraday to roughly 89.15 and settled 91.110, while Brent fell 2.6% to about 99.63 and closed at 102.250, down just 0.06%. Goldman Sachs estimates the release offsets only around half the recent diesel rise. This is the specific fact that moved GER40 from SHORT to RANGE and that keeps USOIL a range with an upward skew.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz closure, Iranian export exhaustion and tanker strikes
catalysts.note: The strait has been effectively closed since the blockade restarted on July 14, with a single commercial transit recorded on September 27 against roughly 85 a day normally. Three facts carry the escalation risk now: Iranian loadings were zero in September with about 15 million barrels left on the water, nearly all bound for China, leaving Tehran roughly two weeks from having nothing to trade; five ships were struck in a 72-hour stretch late last week including a supertanker that caught fire off Oman; and Trump rejected Iran's seven-day ceasefire and phased-reopening proposal, naming the November 3 midterms as the point after which strikes are possible. Iran's conditions were a lifted naval blockade, waived oil sanctions and a ceasefire including Lebanon.

catalysts.event: French 2027 budget passage and the OAT-Bund spread
catalysts.note: The binding constraint on the euro and it is fiscal rather than monetary. Lecornu presented the 2027 draft on October 1: public-sector wages and all but the lowest pensions frozen, consolidation split roughly 60/40 between spending cuts and revenue, the deficit trimmed only from 5.4% to 5.0% of GDP, the EU 3% threshold deferred to 2029, debt at 121.7% and an extra EUR10bn of debt service attributed to the geopolitical backdrop. It faces a parliament that has already unseated one Macron prime minister and landed alongside violent student protests. TE closes the OAT at 4.8656% against a Bund at 3.4545%, about 141bp and the widest since the 2012 crisis, with France now wide of Italy at 4.6107% and Greece at 4.5247%. A spread through 150bp turns EUR bearish; credible passage removes the constraint.

catalysts.event: Escondida strike mediation and the copper supply balance
catalysts.note: BHP's Escondida, the world's largest copper mine, halted all operations on September 23 after a contractor was killed, removing roughly 3,455 tonnes a day, and its supervisors have voted 95% to authorise a strike with mandatory mediation to run first. The asymmetry is in the outcome: a short disruption resolved in mediation leaves supply fundamentally intact, while a month-long stoppage against roughly 39 days of global inventory cover is a materially different shock. Shanghai stocks are low into the October 1-8 Golden Week and the LME prompt spread hit a monthly high on Chinese Q4 smelter maintenance. Copper still fell 3.10% on the week, which is why it is a range and why AUD stays at 0.

catalysts.event: European gas prices and the energy inflation channel
catalysts.note: The leg of the energy shock that transmits to policy rather than to risk appetite, and the one the oil release does not obviously fix. EU gas closed at 74.76 EUR/MWh and German gas at 75.77, up 1.11% and 1.06% on the day and up 137.80% and 130.95% year on year; UK gas is 188.10 GBp/thm, up 2.76% on the week and 154.84% year to date, with the domestic unit rate stepping from 6.29p to 8p per kWh on October 1, about 27% higher year on year. This is why euro area energy inflation surged to 18.8% y/y and contributed roughly 1.7 points of the 3.8% September HICP, and why Bailey's energy condition keeps being met rather than relieved.

geopolitics: The transmission chain from the Gulf to this board acquired a policy response this week, and that is the change. On October 2 the G7 and partner countries agreed with the IEA to release up to 100 million barrels of crude and diesel over four months, beginning immediately and front-loaded with a substantial diesel component across the first 20 days, alongside coordinated refinery maintenance schedules and a commitment not to restrict energy trade; Reuters reported beforehand that the United States had demanded France and Germany draw on their emergency diesel reserves and had threatened to ban diesel exports if they refused. The market's verdict is more useful than the announcement. WTI fell about 4% intraday to roughly 89.15 and settled at 91.110, down 1.90%; Brent fell 2.6% to about 99.63 and closed at 102.250, down 0.06%, up 4.94% on the week and 7.05% on the month. A waterborne crude market that fully round-trips the largest coordinated release since March is not a market whose risk premium is about to break, and Goldman Sachs estimates the release offsets only around half the recent diesel rise. The $11.14 Brent-WTI spread remains the precise statement of where the premium sits, and the release - aimed at the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and refined products - lands on the Cushing side rather than the waterborne side, which is why the spread should stay wide. The reason the premium holds is on the physical and political side of the ledger. The strait has been effectively closed since the blockade restarted on July 14, with a single commercial transit recorded on September 27 against roughly 85 a day under normal conditions. Iranian loadings were zero in September with about 15 million barrels left on the water, nearly all bound for China, which leaves Tehran roughly two weeks from having nothing left to trade - an exhaustion point, and exhaustion is not a de-escalation. Five ships were struck in a 72-hour stretch late last week, including a supertanker that caught fire off Oman. The negotiating track has broken rather than stalled: Iran offered a seven-day ceasefire and phased reopening conditional on the US lifting its naval blockade, waiving oil sanctions and observing a ceasefire extending to Lebanon, Trump rejected it, and he named the November 3 midterms as the point after which renewed strikes are possible. That is the date to hold, and it is also the RBA meeting. The FX reads follow directly. USOIL stays a RANGE but with an upward skew inside it rather than a neutral one, because the release is real supply landing on exactly this contract while the escalation risk is dated rather than removed - and being short crude into an intervention the market has already rejected is the wrong side. Canada gets less help than a 102-dollar Brent print implies, and now slightly less than last week, because the relief is concentrated in the barrels and products Canada sells; CAD therefore stays at -1 on domestic data, with October 9 employment the test. The gas leg is the one the oil release does not obviously fix and the one that transmits to policy: EU gas closed at 74.76 EUR/MWh and German gas at 75.77, up 137.80% and 130.95% year on year, while UK gas is 188.10 GBp/thm and up 154.84% year to date with the domestic unit rate stepping from 6.29p to 8p per kWh on October 1. That is why euro area energy inflation surged to 18.8% y/y and contributed roughly 1.7 points of the 3.8% September HICP, and why Bailey's condition - that the longer energy volatility persists the more likely the Bank needs to raise Bank Rate - keeps being met. The war is the inflation story in Europe, and this week it is what pushed BoE November pricing to 75-88% and moved Breeden and Lombardelli. The haven read is unchanged from last week and still the most counterintuitive observation here: with the strait shut and tankers burning, gold fell 3.38% on the week to 4140.19 and silver 6.06% to 60.365, while the Swiss franc was the firmest major after the dollar - USD/CHF up just 0.06% while EUR/CHF fell 1.14% and CAD/CHF 0.72%. A 5.2830% nominal ten-year with the TIPS real yield edging toward 2.5% taxes a non-yielding haven in a way it does not tax a funding currency whose own policy rate is the comparison being made. So the haven bid is alive and it has migrated: short bullion, respect the franc, and keep the franc crosses as level trades rather than longs. For European equities the release splits the two indices for the first time in weeks - it directly attacks the energy input that justified the GER40 short, which moves that to a range, while the EU50 keeps its own bear case in a banking sector that lagged on a 1.07% up day.
